overview: Twentieth-century Copenhagen became a meeting place for physicists working on quantum theory. This focused chapter follows the institute, discussions and everyday arrangements that helped international collaboration take root.

items.text: Bohr's Institute for Theoretical Physics was dedicated in Copenhagen in March 1921, after fundraising and approval of the project.
During the 1920s, visiting researchers exchanged ideas in Copenhagen. Discussions could happen in small groups and at dinners with the Bohr family.
In 1927, Bohr presented complementarity: different experimental arrangements can require different, mutually exclusive descriptions of a quantum phenomenon. The proposal became a focus of debate.
In the 1930s, a new mathematics institute was built beside the physics institute. Shared classrooms and a canteen were intended to support closer collaboration.
